questions.prompt: Shabib asks why the posterior of a 2 km rural district spans rates from 0.06 to 0.5 bursts per km-year, while a 180 km urban district's spans 0.07 to 0.10, although both used the same prior and five years of data. What is the reason?
options: The rural district's few bursts give a flat likelihood, so the prior shapes much of its posterior
The rural district's prior was wider because it is rural
The sampler mixed worse for the rural district
Rural rates are more variable by nature, whatever the data say
questions.explanation: Exposure of 10 km-years holds a handful of bursts, which constrains the rate weakly; 900 km-years constrain it sharply.
misconceptions: Thinks different widths require different priors, when the same prior was used
Blames the computation for what is a property of the data
Confuses uncertainty about a rate with variability of the process

questions.prompt: You simulate a year of bursts for a district with a rate of 0.2 bursts per km-year and 15 km of mains. Which line simulates one year?
options: rng.poisson(0.2)
rng.poisson(0.2 * 15)
rng.poisson(0.2) * 15
rng.normal(0.2 * 15, 1)
questions.explanation: The expected count is the rate times the exposure, 3 bursts, and the count is a Poisson draw with that mean.
misconceptions: Forgets the exposure: the rate is per kilometre
Scales a count drawn for one kilometre, which gives only multiples of 15
Uses a continuous distribution for a count that cannot be negative or fractional

questions.prompt: A contractor uses Normal(0, 10) on the log burst rate "to let the data speak". Its prior predictive simulation puts 37% of district-years above 500 bursts. What do you conclude?
options: The prior is harmless because the data will overwhelm it
The prior should be widened further to be safe
The prior is informative in an absurd direction and should be replaced by one that rules out impossible rates
The simulation is wrong because priors cannot predict data
questions.explanation: A prior that predicts impossible data carries strong, wrong information; with little data, as in small districts, it moves the posterior.
misconceptions: Assumes data always dominate, which fails for districts with few bursts
Believes wider is always more neutral
Does not know that a prior and a likelihood together imply a distribution of data

questions.prompt: Which reason for the prior α ~ Normal(log 0.1, 1) on the log burst rate meets the course's standard?
options: It is weakly informative
It is the default of the library
It is centred on the engineers' one burst per 10 km a year, and 73% of the network totals it simulates fall in their plausible range of 300 to 3,000
It gave the best fit to the five years of counts
questions.explanation: A reason quotes the knowledge the prior encodes and a check of what it predicts.
misconceptions: Gives a label in place of a reason
Defers to software defaults that know nothing of pipes
Tunes the prior to the same data the model will fit, using the data twice

questions.prompt: Why can Hamiltonian Monte Carlo explore a posterior with 150 parameters where a random-walk sampler stalls?
options: It evaluates the posterior on a fine grid
It uses the gradient of the log posterior to make long moves that stay in regions of high density
It discards most draws so that the rest are independent
It assumes the posterior is normal
questions.explanation: Momentum and the gradient carry the sampler far in one iteration along the shape of the posterior, so proposals are accepted often even in many dimensions.
misconceptions: Confuses sampling with grid evaluation, which is impossible in 150 dimensions
Mistakes thinning for what makes a sampler efficient
Confuses HMC with a normal approximation

questions.prompt: In log E[bursts] = log km + α + Xβ, the coefficient of log km is fixed at 1, so exp(β) for asbestos cement is a ratio of burst rates per kilometre-year.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With the offset, the other terms model the rate per unit of exposure.
misconceptions: Thinks the material coefficient compares total counts, which would mix material with network length

questions.prompt: A fit of four chains shows no divergences, bulk ESS of 7 for α and R-hat of 1.60. Three chains have a mean α near -2.41 and the fourth near -1.23. What do you do?
options: Report the pooled mean of the four chains
Drop the fourth chain and report the other three
Treat the fit as untrustworthy, rerun four chains with full warm-up from dispersed starts, and check again
Accept it, since there are no divergences
questions.explanation: Chains that disagree have not converged to one distribution; only a fresh run that passes the checks can be read.
misconceptions: Averages over chains that sample different things
Discards evidence of a problem without knowing which chains are right
Treats the absence of divergences as proof of convergence

questions.prompt: Zaina's fit hit the maximum tree depth in a third of its draws, with R-hat 1.002, bulk ESS above 1,400 and no divergences. Juhaina asks whether the numbers can be used. What do you answer?
options: Yes: capped trees cost sampling time, and the mixing diagnostics show the draws are sound
No: any warning invalidates a fit
No: the tree depth must never be capped
Only after converting the fit to a variational approximation
questions.explanation: Tree depth is an efficiency diagnostic; validity is judged by R-hat, ESS, divergences and E-BFMI, which all pass.
misconceptions: Treats every warning as a validity failure
Confuses a slow setting with a wrong one
Thinks an approximation is more reliable than a sound sampler

questions.prompt: An inspectorate has 200 schools; 70 have been inspected once. You must estimate each school's rate of serious findings. Which model lets the data decide how much the schools inspected once borrow from the others?
options: A separate rate for each school
One rate for all schools
School rates drawn from a common distribution whose spread is estimated
A separate rate for each school, with the once-inspected schools removed
questions.explanation: Partial pooling estimates the spread between schools, and each school's estimate borrows in proportion to how little data it has.
misconceptions: Trusts one inspection as much as five, so once-inspected schools get extreme estimates
Assumes all schools are alike, which the analyst decides rather than the data
Throws away the schools that most need an estimate

questions.prompt: In a partial-pooling model of 140 districts, which district's estimate moves furthest towards the common rate?
options: A 200 km urban district with 90 bursts in five years
A 2 km rural district with 2 bursts in five years
A 50 km suburban district with 20 bursts
All move by the same amount, set by τ
questions.explanation: Shrinkage depends on how much information a district's own data carry; 2 bursts carry little, so the population dominates.
misconceptions: Thinks large districts are pulled most because they dominate the average
Picks a middle case without reasoning about information
Believes τ shrinks every district equally regardless of its data

questions.prompt: Your partial-pooling model has no predictors. Rural districts, with old asbestos-cement mains, have few bursts each; most of the network is urban. What should worry you before the estimates feed a re-piping plan?
options: Nothing: partial pooling is the recommended model for unequal groups
That rural estimates are shrunk towards a mostly urban rate, which may understate their risk
That urban districts are shrunk too much
That the sampler will diverge on the rural districts
questions.explanation: Shrinkage pulls small districts towards the population mean; if that mean is dominated by a different kind of district, their risk is understated systematically.
misconceptions: Treats a method's standard status as a defence of its effect on a specific group
Reverses who is shrunk: large districts keep their own estimates
Confuses a statistical bias with a computational problem

questions.prompt: Adding pipe material and age to the mean of the district effects reduced τ from 0.56 to 0.41. Which statement follows?
options: Material and age explain about half of the between-district variance, and districts are now shrunk towards a prediction for their pipes
The districts are now pooled less
Material and age are proven causes of bursts
The model fits worse, because τ fell
questions.explanation: 1 - 0.41²/0.56² is about 0.47; with predictors the shrinkage target is the predicted rate for each district.
misconceptions: Reads a smaller spread as weaker pooling
Reads an association in observational data as a proven cause
Thinks a smaller unexplained spread is a worse fit

questions.prompt: Adding an indicator for rural districts to the model of reported bursts will move the rural estimates towards their true burst rates, because it lets rural districts have their own level.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The indicator learns the low reported counts of rural districts, most without sensors, so it moves the estimates of true rates further down.
misconceptions: Assumes a predictor fitted to recorded data corrects a recording problem

questions.prompt: A centred hierarchical model of 49 small districts reports 59 divergences, all at small values of τ. Why there?
options: Small τ forces every district effect into a narrow region, where the step size tuned for the rest of the posterior is far too large
The data are wrong for the districts with small τ
Small τ means the prior is too narrow and must be widened
The sampler ran out of draws
questions.explanation: In the centred form the posterior has a funnel: its width shrinks with τ, so a step size suited to the mouth diverges in the neck.
misconceptions: Blames the data for a geometry of the parameterisation
Confuses a property of the posterior's shape with a prior that is too narrow
Thinks divergences come from too few draws

questions.prompt: Raising target_accept to 0.99 removed all divergences of a centred hierarchical model, but R-hat is 1.14. What do you conclude?
options: The fit is now trustworthy
The chains still disagree; rewrite the model in non-centred form
Run more chains until R-hat falls below 1.01 by chance
Report the fit with a note about R-hat
questions.explanation: No divergences is necessary, not sufficient; disagreeing chains show the posterior is still not explored, and the cause is the geometry.
misconceptions: Treats the absence of divergences as proof of a sound fit
Hopes more chains fix a geometry problem
Publishes numbers from chains that have not converged

questions.prompt: The centred and non-centred forms of a hierarchical model describe the same joint distribution of the data and the parameters.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Only the variables the sampler moves in change: η = μ + τ z with z standard normal has the distribution Normal(μ, τ).
misconceptions: Thinks non-centring changes the model's assumptions rather than its coordinates

questions.prompt: In the model with a reporting share for districts without sensors, the posterior of the reporting share is almost identical to its Beta(14, 6) prior. What does that mean?
options: The model failed and must be refitted
The counts cannot separate the burst rate from the reporting share, so the audit behind the prior carries the correction
The reporting share is exactly 0.70 in every district
The prior was too wide
questions.explanation: Only the product of rate and reporting share reaches the counts; the split comes from the prior, so its source must be stated.
misconceptions: Takes a posterior equal to the prior as a computational failure
Confuses the prior's mean with a known value
Thinks a narrower prior would make the data informative

questions.prompt: Bursts in districts without sensors are reported with probability p. Which likelihood for the reported count y of district j in a year follows?
options: y ~ Poisson(km_j × rate_j)
y ~ Poisson(km_j × rate_j × p_j)
y ~ Poisson(km_j × rate_j) × p_j
y ~ Poisson(km_j × rate_j / p_j)
questions.explanation: Thinning each burst with probability p keeps a Poisson count with its mean multiplied by p.
misconceptions: Ignores the recording process
Multiplies a count by a probability, which gives non-integer counts
Inverts the thinning

questions.prompt: A Poisson model of daily ambulance calls per station is fitted. Which posterior predictive check is most likely to reveal a problem the fit itself could hide?
options: The total number of calls over the year
The mean number of calls per station
The variance of each station's daily calls divided by their mean
The number of stations
questions.explanation: The rates are fitted to reproduce totals and means; the ratio of variance to mean is not forced by the fit, and a Poisson fixes it at 1.
misconceptions: Checks a statistic the fitted rates reproduce by construction
Checks a statistic the fitted rates reproduce by construction
Confuses a property of the design with a property of the data

questions.prompt: A posterior predictive check of the share of zero counts gives p = 0.12. What does this say?
options: The model is wrong with 88% probability
The observed share sits within the range the model produces, towards its edge
The model is right with 12% probability
The check failed and must be repeated with more draws
questions.explanation: The p-value is the share of replicates at least as extreme as the data; 0.12 means the data are not unusual under the model, though near the edge of what it produces.
misconceptions: Reads a predictive p-value as the probability that the model is wrong
Reads a predictive p-value as the probability that the model is right
Treats a moderate p-value as a computational failure

questions.prompt: A negative binomial with mean 4 and shape φ = 8 replaces a Poisson with mean 4. What is the variance of each?
options: Poisson 4, negative binomial 6
Both 4
Poisson 4, negative binomial 32
Poisson 16, negative binomial 6
questions.explanation: A Poisson's variance equals its mean; the negative binomial's is mean + mean²/φ = 4 + 16/8 = 6.
misconceptions: Thinks the same mean implies the same variance
Multiplies the mean by the shape instead of dividing its square
Squares the Poisson's mean

questions.prompt: Two models of clinic waiting times: elpd -2,150 (SE 40) and -2,180 (SE 42); the difference is 30 with a standard error of 8. Which reading is right?
options: No clear difference, because 30 is smaller than either SE
The first predicts held-out patients clearly better: the difference is almost four of its own standard errors
The second is better because its SE is larger
The comparison is invalid unless both have the same number of parameters
questions.explanation: The models share most of their noise, so the difference is judged against the standard error of the difference, not against each model's own SE.
misconceptions: Compares the difference with each model's own SE
Reads a larger SE as better
Thinks leave-one-out needs models of equal size; it already accounts for complexity

questions.prompt: Leave-one-out flags one school-year with Pareto k = 1.1: a fire closed the school for a term and inspections found many problems. What should the analyst do first?
options: Delete the school-year so the warning disappears
Ignore it: one point cannot matter among 800
Confirm what happened, keep the real event, and prefer a model that is not overturned by such years
Raise the number of draws until k falls below 0.7
questions.explanation: A high k says one point moves the posterior a lot; a real event is kept and modelled, while an error would be corrected.
misconceptions: Removes inconvenient real data and understates risk
Thinks one influential point cannot change the conclusions
Treats k as a sampling problem that more draws fix

questions.prompt: A report justifies a model by an R² of 0.91 between observed and fitted counts. Why is this weak evidence?
options: R² cannot be computed for counts
It rewards fitting the data already seen; a model with more parameters always scores higher
0.91 is too low for count data
R² is a frequentist measure and cannot be used with a Bayesian model
questions.explanation: Agreement with the data used to fit says little about prediction; leave-one-out scores each point by a model that did not see it.
misconceptions: Thinks R² is undefined for counts
Thinks a higher threshold would make in-sample fit convincing
Rejects a measure because of its school rather than what it measures

questions.prompt: In a simulation-based calibration, a parameter's rank histogram rises steadily from left to right. What does it indicate?
options: The posterior is too wide
The code is correct
The sampler needs more chains
The posterior is systematically below the true value: the truth's rank is usually high
questions.explanation: A rank counts the draws below the truth; many high ranks mean most draws are below it, so the posterior is biased downwards.
misconceptions: Confuses a slope with a hump
Reads any smooth histogram as uniform
Treats a bias in the model as a sampler setting

questions.prompt: A colleague simulated one dataset from known parameters, fitted her model and recovered both inside their 90% intervals. She says the code is verified. What is the best reply?
options: Agreed: recovering both parameters is the standard test
Repeat with a larger dataset and the code is verified
One run can pass by luck; rank the truth over many simulated datasets and check the ranks are uniform
Verification is impossible for Bayesian models
questions.explanation: A wrong model can cover the truth on one dataset and a right one misses 10% of the time; only the distribution of ranks over many runs tests the code.
misconceptions: Treats one recovery as proof
Thinks more data per run replaces more runs
Believes Bayesian code cannot be tested

questions.prompt: A model passes simulation-based calibration. Which error could it still contain?
options: A prior written with a variance where the scale belongs, in the model only
A likelihood that assumes Poisson counts when the real data are overdispersed
A wrong parameterisation of the negative binomial in the model only
A sampler that cannot reach part of the posterior
questions.explanation: Calibration tests the model against its own simulator; a wrong assumption about the world, made in both, passes. Predictive checks against real data find it.
misconceptions: Misses that a mismatch between model and simulator is exactly what calibration finds
Misses that a mismatch between model and simulator is exactly what calibration finds
Misses that a sampler failing to explore distorts the ranks

questions.prompt: Power-scaling the priors by 0.8 and 1.25 moves the posterior mean of a district's rate by 0.6 posterior standard deviations. What does that suggest?
options: The prior is doing a large share of the work for this quantity; report it and test alternatives
The data dominate the priors for this quantity
The sampler has not converged
The rate must be removed from the report
questions.explanation: A shift of more than a fraction of a posterior sd when the prior is slightly weakened or strengthened means the answer depends on the prior.
misconceptions: Reads a large shift as a small one
Confuses prior sensitivity with a convergence problem
Thinks a prior-sensitive quantity cannot be reported

questions.prompt: Three priors on the spread between districts give the same 15 riskiest districts, but the reporting share of districts without sensors comes only from an audit-based prior. What belongs in the memo?
options: The results are robust to the priors
Nothing about priors: the manager does not need them
The spread prior does not change the plan; the reporting prior carries the rural estimates and rests on one audit
Replace the reporting prior with a flat one to be objective
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is a property of each prior and question; the prior the data cannot check must be named with its source.
misconceptions: Generalises from the priors tested to all of them
Hides the assumption that drives part of the answer
Thinks a flat prior is neutral when the data cannot identify the quantity
